prompt.brief: Design a multi-tenant job scheduling service that runs one-time and recurring jobs reliably, even when schedules spike, workers fail, or a dispatcher is restarted.
successSignals: Separate schedule management, due-work detection, dispatch, and execution.
Explain timing semantics, duplicate delivery, retries, time zones, and missed runs.
Use durable state and leases so dispatcher and worker failures recover safely.
Make tenant fairness, backpressure, idempotency, and operational visibility explicit.

functional: Create, update, pause, resume, and delete one-time or recurring schedules.
Run HTTP, container, or queue-backed jobs with configurable timeout and retry policy.
Support cron-like expressions, time zones, start/end windows, and misfire policy.
Expose execution history, current state, manual run, cancellation, and dead-letter replay.
Isolate tenants with quotas, concurrency limits, authorization, and audit events.
nonFunctional: Provide at-least-once execution with a clear idempotency contract; exactly-once side effects are the job owner's responsibility.
Target p99 dispatch lateness below 10 seconds for jobs within the normal capacity envelope.
Survive dispatcher, worker, queue, and storage node failures without silently losing a due job.
Keep schedule writes strongly consistent while allowing dashboards and metrics to be eventually consistent.
Apply backpressure and tenant fairness instead of allowing one customer to exhaust all workers.
scaleAssumptions: 10 million active schedules, with 100 million executions per day.
Average execution rate is about 1.2K jobs/second; peak bursts reach 10K jobs/second.
Most schedules are recurring and produce a small schedule row plus one execution record per run.
Jobs are external work: median runtime is 5 seconds, with a 15-minute maximum lease and timeout.

metrics.label: Average execution rate
metrics.description: 100M daily executions divided across a 24-hour day.

metrics.label: Peak dispatch rate
metrics.description: Burst budget for aligned cron boundaries and catch-up work.

metrics.label: Active schedules
metrics.description: The due-time index must be sharded; a full-table scan is not viable.

metrics.label: Execution history
metrics.description: Use retention tiers and archive old records instead of keeping all history hot.

entities.name: Schedule
entities.notes: The schedule is the source of truth; version changes fence stale dispatchers and update the indexed next-run entry.

entities.name: Execution
entities.notes: One logical run can have multiple attempts. The idempotency key remains stable across retries.

entities.name: RetryPolicy
entities.notes: Keep policy with the schedule version so a retry is evaluated against the intended configuration.

entities.name: PartitionLease
entities.notes: Short leases and fencing tokens prevent two dispatcher instances from owning a partition after a pause or network split.

apis.contract: { job, trigger, retryPolicy, concurrencyPolicy } -> { scheduleId, nextRunAt }
apis.notes: Require tenant authorization and an idempotency key; validate time zone and cron expression before the atomic write.
Use an expected version to avoid lost updates and atomically move the due-time index.
Read from an execution index; do not scan the scheduler's hot due-time partitions.
Manual runs share the normal queue and idempotency path, but are marked as operator-triggered.

dataFlow.title: Persist the schedule
dataFlow.description: Validate the trigger, authorize the tenant, calculate the first next-run timestamp, and write the schedule plus its due-time index entry in one conditional operation.

dataFlow.title: Claim due work
dataFlow.description: A dispatcher owns a leased shard, reads a bounded time window, and conditionally claims each due schedule using its version and a run identity.

dataFlow.title: Enqueue an execution
dataFlow.description: Create an execution record and publish a durable message. A transactional outbox or idempotent publisher closes the gap between the database write and queue publish.

dataFlow.title: Execute with a lease
dataFlow.description: A fair worker consumes the message, acquires or renews the execution lease, invokes the target, and records success or a retryable failure.

dataFlow.title: Advance or recover
dataFlow.description: On success, compute the next occurrence. On failure, apply backoff and jitter; after the retry budget, move the execution to a dead-letter state and alert the tenant.

architecture.title: Distributed job scheduler reference architecture
architecture.summary: A durable schedule store feeds a partitioned dispatcher, which claims due work and hands it to queues so execution remains reliable under retries and worker churn.

layers.label: Control plane
layers.description: Clients create, inspect, pause, and change schedules.

layers.label: Dispatch plane
layers.description: Due schedules are discovered, claimed, and converted into durable execution messages.

layers.label: Execution plane
layers.description: Workers execute jobs with leases, retries, and result recording.

keyPaths.label: Schedule path
keyPaths.description: Create or update a schedule and atomically maintain its next-run index.

keyPaths.label: Dispatch path
keyPaths.description: Partition owners claim due entries and enqueue execution attempts.

keyPaths.label: Retry and recovery path
keyPaths.description: Failed attempts are rescheduled with backoff or moved to a dead-letter queue for inspection.

components.label: Schedule Store
components.description: Durable source of truth for schedules, policies, ownership, and lifecycle state.

components.label: Due-Time Index
components.description: Sharded index ordered by next-run time so dispatchers can scan bounded windows.

components.label: Dispatcher Fleet
components.description: Leases partitions, claims due schedules, and creates one execution message per run.

components.label: Execution Queue
components.description: Durably buffers runnable attempts and isolates schedule spikes from worker capacity.

components.description: Executes jobs within tenant limits, renews leases, and reports success or failure.

components.label: Execution Store
components.description: Records attempts, idempotency keys, outcomes, retry state, and dead-letter references.

components.description: Tracks lateness, queue depth, retries, worker saturation, and missed-run alerts.

deepDives.title: Finding due schedules
points: Index by time buckets and hash shards so dispatchers read only a narrow window.
Use a lease per partition with fencing tokens; a lock alone is unsafe during pauses and network partitions.
Allow a small look-ahead window and recheck schedule version and status before enqueueing.

deepDives.title: At-least-once execution
points: A worker can finish a side effect and crash before acknowledging the queue, so duplicates are unavoidable.
Pass a stable execution idempotency key to the job and require downstream writes to deduplicate it.
Record attempt state with conditional transitions so late acknowledgements cannot overwrite a newer retry.

deepDives.title: Recurring schedules and misfires
points: Store the schedule's time zone and compute occurrences with a tested library; never treat local time as UTC implicitly.
Define skip, run-once, or catch-up behavior when a schedule is paused or the system is down.
Bound catch-up work to protect the queue and expose skipped occurrences as observable state.

deepDives.title: Fairness and backpressure
points: Partition queue capacity by tenant or weighted fair scheduling so a noisy customer cannot starve others.
Enforce per-tenant concurrency and global admission limits before invoking external jobs.
Scale workers from queue age and lateness, not only queue depth, because long jobs hide waiting time.

tradeoffs.title: Polling vs timing wheel
tradeoffs.recommendation: Start with sharded time buckets and bounded polling; introduce a timing wheel when sub-second precision or very high schedule density justifies it.
tradeoffs.caution: A timing wheel reduces scans but adds complexity around persistence, recovery, and long-duration timers.

tradeoffs.title: Queue-first vs database-first dispatch
tradeoffs.recommendation: Create an execution record before publishing and use an outbox or reconciliation worker to guarantee eventual publication.
tradeoffs.caution: Queue-first is simpler to scale but can lose the durable record needed for audit and deduplication.

tradeoffs.title: Exactly-once vs at-least-once
tradeoffs.recommendation: Promise at-least-once delivery and make idempotency explicit at the execution boundary.
tradeoffs.caution: Exactly-once claims usually hide an external side-effect boundary that the scheduler cannot atomically control.

commonMistakes: Using one global lock or scanning every schedule each second.
Claiming a schedule without fencing stale dispatcher instances.
Assuming queue acknowledgement means the external job side effect happened exactly once.
Ignoring daylight-saving transitions, missed runs, and bounded catch-up.
Letting retries bypass tenant concurrency limits or overwhelm a downstream service.

followUps.question: How do you recover after a dispatcher is down for ten minutes?
followUps.answer: A new owner acquires the partition lease, scans from the last durable watermark, applies the schedule's misfire policy, and publishes bounded catch-up work while reporting lateness.

followUps.question: How would you support millions of jobs at the same timestamp?
followUps.answer: Hash schedules across many time-bucket shards, spread enqueue work with jitter where semantics allow it, and apply tenant and global admission limits.

followUps.question: How do you cancel a running job?
followUps.answer: Mark the execution cancelled with a conditional update, send a cancellation signal when the worker supports it, and fence late completion updates; forceful termination remains target-specific.

followUps.question: What must be monitored?
followUps.answer: Track dispatch lateness, due-item age, queue age, lease expirations, retry rate, dead letters, per-tenant saturation, and the gap between persisted executions and published messages.

rubric.description: Separates schedule lifecycle, due-time discovery, durable dispatch, and worker execution with a readable critical path.
Explains leases, fencing, retries, idempotency, duplicate delivery, outbox recovery, and failure transitions.
Uses explicit capacity assumptions, sharded indexes, bounded scans, backpressure, and tenant-aware concurrency.
Covers time zones, recurring rules, misfires, catch-up, cancellation, manual runs, and retention.
Defines lateness and completion SLOs plus metrics and operator workflows for dead letters and stuck leases.
